title: A Hearing, a Plot, an Escape
overview: Paul's hearing before Jerusalem's ruling council collapses into chaos, more than forty men plot to kill him, and a Roman commander has him moved under heavy guard to the governor in Caesarea.

parts.label: Struck before the council (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The high priest had Paul hit on the mouth as soon as he claimed a clear conscience, breaking the very law the council existed to uphold. Paul called him a wall painted white, meaning a fake whose clean surface hides rot, and warned that God would strike him.

parts.label: Paul's surprising apology (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: When rebuked, Paul said he had not realized this was the high priest and quoted a law against speaking evil of a ruler. Scholars are unsure why he did not know; the office changed hands often, Paul had been away for years, and some read his words as irony.

parts.label: The council splits (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: The Pharisees believed the dead would rise and that angels and spirits exist, while the Sadducees, the party of the leading priests, denied all this. By saying he was on trial over the hope of resurrection, which for Paul centered on Jesus rising, he split the council so badly that Roman soldiers had to pull him out by force.

parts.label: A promise in the night (v. 11)
parts.note: Jesus appears to Paul and tells him he will speak about him in Rome, just as he has in Jerusalem. This promise shapes the rest of the book, which follows Paul's long road to Rome.

parts.label: A murder plot uncovered (vv. 12-22)
parts.note: More than forty men swore not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul, and asked the leading priests to help lure him into an ambush. Paul's sister's son heard of it and warned him, and the commander taking the boy by the hand suggests he was young.

parts.label: Sent by night to Caesarea (vv. 23-35)
parts.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was where the Roman governor lived, and the commander sent hundreds of soldiers to get Paul there safely by night. His letter says the dispute was about Jewish religious law, not a crime, and flatters his own role, claiming he rescued Paul as a Roman citizen though he actually learned this only afterward.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Paul's sharp words to the high priest and his move to divide the council were honest courage or a moment where he fell short.
think: Paul claims a clear conscience while powerful people are sure he is wrong; how far do you trust your own conscience when those around you disagree?
